overview: Tenacity 6.0's HackerDetector is a wire-silent observer that never observes. The module creates a DetectionManager holding three detections (ReachA, FlightA, FlightB), and its TickEvent handler iterates mc.theWorld.getLoadedEntityList() and the detection list, but it never calls runCheck on any detection: every line of the handler renders detectionManager.getDetections() through ChatUtil.hacker, a client-side chat line, so toggling the module spams the local chat with the same list object over and over. No packet is sent or received. The three detections behind it are the real framework: FlightA tests for hover, FlightB tests for sustained air time, and ReachA is a stub that always returns false. The brief's S02 pin describes the death-message chat trigger of the wider HackerDetect family; this module has no chat or packet trigger of any kind, so the pinned surface is covered in prose and the packets list reflects the entity state the module reads instead.

sections.p: Detection is an abstract class with a name, a category and an abstract runCheck(EntityPlayer). DetectionManager's constructor registers three instances: ReachA under the combat category, and FlightA and FlightB under movement. The module's onTick handler, bound by the EventSubscriberPool when the module is enabled, walks the loaded entity list and the detection list in nested loops but only prints; the inner loop bodies are empty of any runCheck invocation. The result is that the checks exist as classes but execute nowhere in the client, and the module's observable behavior is a chat spammer printing the same ArrayList.toString every tick, gated only by the world and player null checks at the top of the handler.

FlightA.runCheck returns !player.onGround && player.motionY == 0 && MovementUtils.isMoving(player), a hover test: airborne, no vertical motion, but moving. FlightB returns player.getAir() > 20 && player.motionY == 0 && MovementUtil.isMoving(), a sustained-air test gated on the client-wide MovementUtil.isMoving(), which reads MC.thePlayer.movementInput and therefore tests whether the LOCAL user is pressing keys, not whether the watched player is moving. That cross-player contamination means FlightB's verdict on a target is partly a function of the user's own key state, a genuine bug worth flagging. ReachA.runCheck returns false unconditionally, so even a working caller would never flag reach; the combat detection is a stub. The air-ticks threshold of 20 and the hover profile are the only substantive heuristics in the package.

sections.h: Wire reality and the pinned surface
sections.p: The module emits and consumes nothing. ChatUtil.hacker writes a ChatComponentText into the in-game chat GUI, a purely local render that never becomes a C01 chat packet. The entity list it reads is populated server-side by spawn, look-and-move and teleport packets, which is why the packets array lists S0C, S14 and S18 as the observed state feeds rather than the brief's S02. In the wider client family this category pairs a detector with an S02-triggered death-insult spammer; the Tenacity module has neither the trigger nor the insult path. The honest consequence for countering is that no server-side check can detect the module, because its entire effect is local rendering, and the entries below are the server-side twins of the behaviors its detections half-implement.

files.label: HackerDetectorModule.java
files.explanation: The module file shows the disconnect between the framework and its use. The constructor registers a MultipleBoolSetting with Flight A, Flight B and Reach A toggles and a DetectionManager; onTick then loops over the loaded entity list and the detection list, but the only statement in the loops is ChatUtil.hacker(String.valueOf(detectionManager.getDetections())), repeated several times. There is no runCheck call anywhere in the file, which is why the module is inert as a detector. The timer field and the BooleanSetting import are unused. The file is the complete proof that the detections are never invoked, and it pairs with DetectionManager.java as the registration side.

files.label: DetectionManager.java (detection registry)
files.explanation: DetectionManager is the registry the module owns but never consults. Its constructor calls addDetections with ReachA, FlightA and FlightB, the three checks the MultipleBoolSetting toggles are named after, and getDetections() returns the ArrayList the module's chat spam renders. The class shows the intended architecture: detections would be pulled from this list inside the entity loop and run through runCheck(player), and the boolean settings would gate them. Because the manager only ever builds the list and the module only ever prints it, the file documents the latent framework rather than an active one, and it is the natural supporting file for the analysis.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (vertical physics envelope)
countering.explanation: NoCheatPlus SurvivalFly rebuilds the allowed vertical envelope from the block cache and never trusts the packet's onGround flag, since ground truth comes from a ray trace at minY minus yOnGround. The module's FlightA and FlightB look for the hover profile (airborne, zero vertical motion, moving), and that profile is exactly what SurvivalFly's vDistRel envelope punishes with a set-back when a real flyer emits it, because the allowed vertical distance initializes from the previous move's momentum and accepts only named envelopes like jumps and steps. The honest framing for this entry is that the check is the server-side twin of the client heuristic: it validates the same property on the same players, but the Tenacity module emits no movement packets of its own, so the envelope never receives a signal from the detector itself.

countering.label: fight Reach (attack distance bound)
countering.explanation: NCP's combat reach check validates attack distance against the survival bound, defaulting to 4.02 blocks in this tree with a reachMod reduce band that silently cancels repeat hits above the limit. The module's ReachA detection is a stub that always returns false, so even the client's own reach heuristic never fires for any player, which makes the server-side reach check the only real gate for the behavior ReachA was meant to expose. The detector is invisible to it because it never attacks: no C02 use-entity packet is sent, FightListener never scores it, and the reach ledger stays untouched. This entry is the honest boundary between the client's dead combat detection and the server's live one.

countering.label: InvalidPitch (look range gate)
countering.explanation: Hawk's InvalidPitch check in the look package is the server-side twin of the pitch-range test that the wider HackerDetect family applies to other players: it punishes any pitch outside the legal range, gated on the movement event having a look delta. The Tenacity module runs its observations on TickEvent against the locally loaded entity list and renders the results through the chat GUI, so the only rotations that reach the server are the user's own, and the check can never see the detector's evaluation of other players. The entry is honest-gap framing in the established wire-silent-observer style: nothing can detect the detector, and this check is the enforcement side of the property the detector half-implements.

countering.label: Speed (movement prediction discrepancy)
countering.explanation: Hawk Speed predicts the next position from the previous move plus friction, applied force and adders, and punishes only moves faster than expected once the horizontal discrepancy passes 0.1, with piston-push exemptions. It is the enforcement side of the flight behavior FlightB half-implements: a player hovering with more than 20 air ticks and zero vertical motion would accumulate discrepancy on every move, because the envelope expects gravity-driven descent. The module never emits a move packet, so the prediction ledger processes nothing from it, and the check stays clean by construction. Both sides of the honest boundary hold: the check catches the cheat the detector looks for, and the detector itself is untraceable because its output never leaves the client.
